introduction-the-plumbing-problem-in-ml.core: Features are model inputs derived from raw data (for example 'average spend over 30 days'). Teams repeatedly re-implement them for training and serving, inconsistently. A feature store centralises feature definitions, computation, storage and serving.

first_principles.problem: Five teams each compute 'user spend last 30 days' differently, and the online and offline versions don't match.
truths: Training and serving need the same logic.
Historical and real-time access patterns differ.
derivation: Guarantee **point-in-time correctness**; enable **reuse** with a registry.

analogy.title: A central kitchen preparing ingredients
analogy.story: Instead of each restaurant chopping its own onions differently, one kitchen prepares standard ingredients for all.
analogy.breaks: Small teams with few models may not need a full feature store.

check.a: A model input derived from raw data, such as a user's transaction count over the last hour.

the-enemy-training-serving-skew.core: Training-serving skew happens when features are computed differently in training (batch SQL in a notebook) and in production (application code), or with different data freshness. The model sees different inputs live than it learned on, and silently degrades.

first_principles.problem: A model scores 0.92 AUC offline and performs poorly in production with no errors, because the 'same' feature is calculated differently.
truths: Skew causes no errors, just bad predictions.
derivation: **Same transformations** materialised to the offline and online stores.
**Log served features** and compare them with the training distribution.

analogy.title: Practising with one ball and playing with another
analogy.story: Training with a soft ball and then playing the match with a hard ball ruins your timing.
analogy.breaks: Some skew comes from data drift, not logic, which also needs monitoring.

example.title: A null-handling skew
flow: Fix: one definition in the feature store

check.a: A mismatch between how features are computed or supplied in training versus in production, which silently degrades model performance.

architecture-online-vs-offline-stores.core: A feature store has two stores. The offline store (a data lake or warehouse, like Parquet, BigQuery or Snowflake) holds full history for training and backfills. The online store (Redis, DynamoDB, Cassandra) holds the latest values for low-latency lookup at inference. Materialisation jobs sync them.

first_principles.problem: A warehouse is too slow for real-time inference, and a key-value store can't hold years of history for training.
truths: Both must derive from the same logic.
derivation: **Materialise** offline → online on schedule or streaming.

analogy.title: An archive and a front-desk drawer
analogy.story: The archive keeps every record for research; the front desk keeps the latest file for instant answers.
analogy.breaks: Keeping two stores in sync adds operational complexity and freshness lag.

example.title: Fetching features at inference
example.outcome: one feature system for two access patterns.

check.q: Why does a feature store need both online and offline stores?
check.a: Training needs large-scale historical data, while inference needs very low-latency access to the latest values.

point-in-time-correctness-time-travel.core: When building training data, each label must be joined only with feature values that were known at that event's time, not later. Point-in-time (as-of) joins prevent data leakage, where future information inflates offline accuracy and then fails in production.

first_principles.problem: Training joins today's 'account balance' to last year's fraud labels, so the model learns from the future and fails live.
truths: Models must learn only from information available at prediction time.
derivation: For each label, take the **latest feature value ≤ label time**.

analogy.title: Judging a past decision with only what was known then
analogy.story: You can't fault a decision using information that only became available later.
analogy.breaks: Point-in-time joins are computationally expensive at scale, so use optimised engines.

code.text:
SELECT l.user_id, l.label, l.ts, f.avg_amount_30d
FROM labels l
ASOF JOIN features f ON l.user_id = f.user_id AND f.ts <= l.ts

check.q: What is data leakage in feature engineering?
check.a: Using information in training that wouldn't have been available at prediction time, inflating offline accuracy.

feature-reuse-and-the-feature-registry.core: The feature registry catalogues every feature (name, definition, owner, entity, source, freshness, version, which models use it), so teams discover and reuse existing features instead of rebuilding them, with consistent semantics and governance.

first_principles.problem: Seven teams build seven versions of 'user 30-day spend', costing duplicated compute and inconsistent results.
derivation: **Register** feature views with metadata and owners.

analogy.title: A shared recipe book in a restaurant group
analogy.story: Chefs reuse tested recipes instead of inventing their own version of the house sauce.
analogy.breaks: A registry full of undocumented features doesn't help, so require descriptions and owners.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Other teams find and reuse it.

code.text:
user_stats = FeatureView(
    name="user_stats", entities=[user], ttl=timedelta(days=2),
    schema=[Field(name="avg_amount_30d", dtype=Float32)],
    source=txn_source, owner="risk-team@acme.io",
    tags={"pii": "false", "description": "Mean transaction amount over 30 days"})

check.q: What's the main benefit of a feature registry?
check.a: Discovery and reuse of existing, consistently defined features across teams, with ownership and governance.
